title: The Scientific Revolution

cards.h: A telescope, an apple story and a very angry Church
cards.b:
In 1609-10, an Italian professor named Galileo pointed a telescope at the sky and saw four moons circling Jupiter. They did not circle Earth. That was a problem for everyone who thought everything did.

This was the beginning of seeing the world with evidence first.
Copernicus published On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres in 1543, placing the Sun at the centre. The same year Vesalius published a book on human anatomy based on dissection.

Johannes Kepler used data from Tycho Brahe to show planets move in ellipses, not perfect circles (1609). Galileo backed Copernicus with telescope sights: Jupiter's moons, Venus's phases, craters on the Moon.

In 1633 the Inquisition forced Galileo to recant. He lived the rest of his life under house arrest.

Isaac Newton published the Principia in 1687. His laws of motion and universal gravitation explained both a falling apple and the orbit of the Moon with the same rules.

That idea, that nature follows mathematical laws that humans can find, changed how people thought.

cards.h: A new way of finding things out
cards.b:
Francis Bacon urged people to learn by experiment and observation. Descartes said to doubt everything and build up through reason. The Royal Society (1660) and the French Academy (1666) spread findings in journals.

Instruments such as the microscope and the barometer opened new worlds.

Many of the scientists were deeply religious. Newton wrote more on alchemy and theology than on physics. Ideas moved slowly, and plenty of old beliefs lasted.

Historians even debate whether to call it a 'revolution'. Some prefer 'a long series of changes'.

cards.h: Did an apple hit Newton's head?
cards.b:
Myth: yes, and he shouted 'Eureka'.Fact: Newton himself later told friends that seeing an apple fall set him thinking about gravity. The head-bonk is a later embellishment.

Another myth: Galileo was tortured or jailed in a dungeon. He wasn't. And 'Yet it moves' is probably a legend.

Kerala's astronomers and Jai Singh

Kerala was doing mathematics that Europe reached later. Madhava of Sangamagrama (c. 1340–1425) found infinite series for sine, cosine and pi, some two centuries before Newton and Leibniz. In 1500 Nilakantha Somayaji wrote the Tantrasangraha, placing the inner planets in orbit round the Sun, which in turn circled the Earth, a model close to Tycho Brahe's.

Sawai Jai Singh II of Jaipur (1688–1743) built observatories called Jantar Mantars at Delhi (1724), Jaipur, Ujjain, Varanasi and Mathura. He studied European tables and bought Jesuit books and telescopes, but built huge stone instruments. They are old Indian astronomy at its last great peak.

Five things to remember

  1. Copernicus (1543) put the Sun at the centre.
  2. Kepler found elliptical orbits; Galileo used the telescope.
  3. Newton's Principia (1687) unified earth and sky.
  4. Experiment and mathematics became the tools.
  5. Kerala's astronomers got there early on series.

Think about it

  • Why does a new tool, like a telescope, change ideas so much?
  • Why might Europe take the credit for ideas from many places?
